text: The Donato family owns judges, lawyers and a few politicians, and none of it helps when a kidnapping goes wrong. What follows is a war inside a household rather than between rivals, which is the harder thing to stage: the people who have to be dealt with are relatives. Leopoldo Torre Nilsson works from precedent. The Galiffi clan, Italian in origin and Fascist in sympathy, took hold of Rosario across the twenties and thirties, a city the film calls the Chicago of Latin America, and that borrowed nickname carries its own argument about what arrives in a country along with its immigrants. It holds a Silver Condor for best film. Two hours is a long stretch in which to watch an organization come apart, and the patience suits the material, since what unravels was assembled over a decade of favours.

The boss has never once had to ask for obedience; it simply arrives. Then one of his own men decides to testify, and the rest of the film is about what that costs everyone still in the room. Fernando Ayala has eighty-six minutes, no space for the crime picture's usual furniture, the heist, the chase, the widening manhunt, so the story stays among a handful of men who go on seeing each other daily. What holds the attention is not who prevails but what the obedience was made of: fear, habit, a cut of the money, the small pleasure of standing near a man who decides things. A witness, after all, has to keep living somewhere. Jefe is a plain word, nearer to foreman than to king, and the film treats it as a post a man can be removed from rather than a rank he owns.

Kazuo Hara does not visit the novelist Mitsuharu Inoue so much as stay. The film runs 157 minutes and covers the last years of Inoue's life, a stretch in which a writer's account of himself and the daily evidence around him are both within reach of a camera, and Hara is interested in the distance between the two. Kinema Junpo named it the best film of its year. Scholarship on Hara has since framed his documentaries as work that produces reality rather than gathering it, which is a courteous way of saying that a camera alters what a subject is willing to be. Nothing in this encounter is neutral. Inoue is a professional maker of versions, in failing health, with readers still listening, and Hara hands him the hours in which to make one more.

Julio Cortázar reads his own sentences on the soundtrack, which settles in advance what kind of documentary this is going to be. Tristán Bauer has eighty minutes and no appetite for the encyclopedia entry: he follows what happened to the writing after it left the writer, how Argentine readers took it up and quarrelled with it as the politics around them shifted. That is a hard thing to photograph, since the events all occur inside other people's reading. The film is poetic in the practical sense, a voice setting the terms and the images obliged to keep up, and the country's changes work as a second subject rather than as background. Eighty minutes is short for a life and about right for an argument about one.

Khuzestan empties house by house in the first months of the war, and one mother will not go. Her older son and the teenage one argue with her every day, and their case is the easy one to state: the neighbours have gone, the roads are still open, staying gets people killed. Hers cannot be made in that register at all. She became a mother in those rooms. Mehdi Jafari builds ninety-four minutes on a war film's least photogenic situation, the family that is still deciding, and keeps the fighting where this family meets it, as pressure from outside the frame on an argument about a house. The Crystal Simorgh for best film went to it. The front never has to appear; a son losing his temper with his mother in a town that has mostly gone carries all of it.

In 1962 Argentina sent to the Academy Awards a film about young people with money and nothing pressing to do. Rodolfo Kuhn took 106 minutes on a subject that resists scenes: middle-class frustration, felt by people whose lives contain no obstacle hard enough to push against. Not the young in general, but a particular set of them, with the leisure to notice their own dissatisfaction and the means to keep it running. The frustration is the plot. A picture built that way has to locate its incidents in talk, in borrowed rooms, in the long stretch after midnight when everybody is still deciding what to do, and it has to stay honest about how little ever gets decided. Los jóvenes viejos observes the boredom without catching it, which is the harder half of the job.

The debts Kanji works off were never his: they came with the marriage, from his wife's father, and they have outlasted her. He farms a poor field and raises a daughter on what it returns. Tomu Uchida gives this 115 minutes in 1939, a great deal of screen time for a man whose plans reach no further than the next season, and the length is the argument: in an agricultural year, debt is not a crisis but a climate. Nothing about the arrangement is unusual in his village, which is why it is worth filming. It topped the Kinema Junpo list for the year. What the picture asks for is a specific sort of attention, to soil, to weather, to the difference one bad harvest makes in a household of two, and it returns that attention as texture rather than as uplift or ruin.

Four men are chosen to walk out through the encirclement while the rest of the unit stays where it is and waits. Being chosen is no honour in that situation; it is a rota. The film is billed as war, drama and adventure, and the third word is the accurate one, since the shape is an errand made on foot by people who cannot be resupplied, cannot signal and must not be seen. Rasoul Mollagholipour spends 115 minutes on it, and the running time goes where the situation sends it: into ground covered slowly, and into the waiting of the men left behind, whose only news will arrive on legs. What the film measures is distance, how far four men can get and how long the position behind them can be asked to hold.

Båstad, 1968: a Davis Cup tie between Sweden and Rhodesia, and a crowd that has come to stop it being played. Roy Andersson gives 102 minutes to the argument rather than the tennis, putting demonstrators and members of the Swedish government on camera in turn and letting each say what sport is for, where politics begins, and when breaking a law is permitted. The interview flatters whoever stays calmest, and much of the tension here comes from watching official language work to keep its composure while the question underneath it refuses to go away. It took the Guldbagge for best film. What lasts is not the fixture but the sound of a small country arguing with itself, in public and on the record, about what a game is allowed to mean.

A doctor rides from Shiraz into Qashqai country to treat his sister's husband, in a season when the roads belong to foreign armies. Masoud Jafari Jozani sets the film in the Allied occupation of Iran during the Second World War, when the central government was one claimant to authority among tribal confederations, elders, rebels and other countries' soldiers, and he moves among all of them behind a useful excuse: medicine gets a man past positions that stop everyone else. Across 116 minutes that structure keeps pulling the story off the political map and back to a family, a younger brother down in the city, a marriage up in the camps. Occupation, as this film has it, is lived as a series of local arrangements: whose permission is needed, whose road it is this week, who is owed a visit.

Everyone in the village is related to everyone else, apart from one vagabond nobody can place. Then a young woman arrives for her first teaching post, and the count of outsiders goes to two. Im Kwon-taek keeps it to 94 minutes and lets the mystery sit in that arrangement rather than in an event: in a settlement high enough that news has nowhere to travel but in circles, nothing can be asked without the asking being noticed. The teacher has standing and no history here. The man has the reverse. A first posting is usually a story about work, and this one is a story about being the only adult in the valley without a cousin, in a place where every household settled its opinion of every other household generations ago.

The bride's father has locked himself in the attic and will not come down for the wedding. Below him the day proceeds: a butcher with money, a taste for liquor and a history with women is marrying a woman a good deal younger, and the house has to manage a celebration around one closed door. Åke Falck keeps both floors in view at once, and that is the design, a private refusal held above a party that cannot acknowledge it and still go on. The shape of the thing is farce. The temperature is not. It has a Guldbagge for best film. Ninety-five minutes in a Swedish house in 1964, with the drink, the money and the age difference all in plain sight and none of them the sort of thing a wedding is permitted to discuss.
